c.tagline: A honey-colored desert city of windcatchers, mud-brick alleys and living Zoroastrian tradition.

taxi.fareNote: Foreign bank and credit cards do NOT work anywhere in Iran — bring cash (USD or EUR) to exchange for rials and carry plenty. Agree the fare before getting in a street taxi, or use the Snapp/Tapsi apps, which are cheaper and priced automatically.

emergency.note: 110 reaches police and 115 is the ambulance/emergency medical line; English is limited, so ask your hotel to help if possible.

avoid.reason: Nothing serious beyond occasional taxi overcharging and motorbikes in the old town's narrow lanes.

hood_desc: The oldest quarter of Yazd, a UNESCO-listed labyrinth of mud-brick alleys, courtyard houses and wind towers around the Fahadan Museum and the 12-Imam shrine; the most atmospheric place to stay, in a restored traditional hotel. Best for soaking up the old city on foot.

The city's landmark public square, dominated by the towering three-story Amir Chakhmaq façade and its rows of arched alcoves, ringed by teahouses, a bazaar and a confectionery district; a central, lively base a short walk from most sights.

The commercial heart around the Jameh Mosque and the covered Grand Bazaar, where lanes of coppersmiths, textile and sweet shops thread between historic caravanserais; the best area for markets and everyday shopping.

A quieter district built around the Dowlatabad Garden, a Persian paradise garden with the tallest windcatcher in the world and reflecting pools; leafy, calm and residential, a little removed from the tourist core.
Yazd's modern hotel and dining strip southeast of the old city, with newer four-star hotels, cafes and easy road access; convenient and comfortable, though it lacks the old-town character.

water.note: Tap water is chlorinated but brackish and mineral-heavy; most visitors drink bottled.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 9:00 PM; there is no metro, so shared and app taxis fill the gaps and cover evenings.
transit.note: Yazd has no metro or tram; getting around is by city bus, cheap shared 'savari' taxis on fixed routes, private taxis and the Snapp/Tapsi ride apps. The compact old city is best explored on foot.
transit.pay: Buses use a rechargeable smart card bought at kiosks; taxis are paid in cash rial (foreign cards don't work). Ride-app fares can be paid in cash to the driver.

bus: Intercity VIP coaches to Isfahan, Shiraz, Tehran and Kerman
train: Yazd railway station on the Tehran-Kerman/Bandar Abbas line (trains to Tehran, Isfahan, Kerman)

transit.m: Snapp or Tapsi ride-hail app to the old city (~15 min)
Airport taxi to the center (~15-20 min); agree the fare first

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving small change for good service is appreciated. Taarof (polite refusal) is common — offer anyway.

food.name: Shooli
food.desc: Yazd's signature sour soup of beetroot, spinach and herbs thickened with flour, finished with vinegar or pomegranate paste. Eaten hot with flatbread.

places.name: Hammam-e Khan Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Restored bathhouse near the bazaar; locals and travellers alike come for shooli and Yazdi stews.

places.name: Termeh and Toranj Restaurant
places.note: Long-running traditional house serving shooli, wheat porridge and other Yazdi home dishes.

places.name: Silk Road Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Courtyard restaurant in the oldest quarter; reliable version of the soup for first-timers.

food.name: Gheymeh Yazdi
food.desc: The local take on gheymeh: split-pea and lamb stew scented with cinnamon and rosewater, sweeter and more fragrant than the Tehran version.

places.name: Hammam-e Khan Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Menu of Yazdi classics including gheymeh Yazdi, dizi and kashk-e bademjan.

places.name: Malek-o Tojjar Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Qajar merchant house with a courtyard dining room and a properly spiced local gheymeh.

places.name: Haji Ashpaz
places.note: Old-school kitchen popular with Yazdi families for stews and rice at everyday prices.

food.name: Qottab
food.desc: Deep-fried almond and walnut pastry crescents perfumed with cardamom and rosewater, dusted in powdered sugar. Yazd's most exported sweet.

places.name: Haj Khalifeh Ali Rahbar Confectionery
places.note: The city's most famous sweet house, over a century old; the benchmark for qottab.

places.name: Haj Khalifeh Rahbar branch
places.note: Central branch handy for buying boxed qottab and baklava after sightseeing.

places.name: Khan Bazaar sweet shops
places.note: Row of traditional confectioners selling qottab by weight, freshly fried each morning.

food.name: Baghlava Yazdi
food.desc: Small diamond-cut baklava of ground almond and pistachio with cardamom and rosewater, softer and less syrupy than Turkish styles.

places.name: Haj Khalifeh Ali Rahbar Confectionery
places.note: Best-known name for Yazdi baklava; boxes travel well and are the classic gift.

places.name: Khan Bazaar sweet shops
places.note: Historic bazaar confectioners where you can taste before buying by the kilo.

places.name: Haj Khalifeh Rahbar branch
places.note: Convenient central counter with the same range of Yazdi sweets.

food.name: Pashmak
food.desc: Persian cotton candy invented in Yazd: sesame-and-sugar floss spun into silky threads, often flavoured with saffron, pistachio or cocoa.

places.name: Haj Khalifeh Ali Rahbar Confectionery
places.note: Sells fresh pashmak alongside the qottab; ask for the saffron version.

places.name: Khan Bazaar sweet shops
places.note: Several stalls spin pashmak on site, so you can watch the threads being pulled.

places.name: Amir Chakhmaq Square confectioners
places.note: Cluster of sweet shops around the square, open late into the evening.

food.name: Faloodeh Yazdi
food.desc: Frozen dessert of thin starch vermicelli in rosewater syrup, served with lime juice or sour cherry; often paired with saffron ice cream.

places.name: Amir Chakhmaq Square ice cream and faloodeh stalls
places.note: Evening ritual spot; locals queue for faloodeh with bastani under the facade.

places.name: Khan Bazaar sweet shops
places.note: Traditional counters serving faloodeh in metal bowls with a squeeze of lime.

places.name: Silk Road Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Easy sit-down option for faloodeh and saffron ice cream after dinner.

food.name: Doogh
food.desc: Salted, lightly fizzy yogurt drink with dried mint, the standard partner to kebab and rice in Yazd's dry desert heat.

places.name: Hammam-e Khan Traditional Restaurant
places.note: House doogh served in metal jugs with the kebab and stew platters.

places.name: Termeh and Toranj Restaurant
places.note: Traditional dining room where doogh comes as a matter of course with the meal.

places.name: Panahandeh Cafe
places.note: Seventy-year-old lentil-soup institution; cheap doogh with a bowl of adasi.

food.name: Saffron and rosewater sharbat
food.desc: Chilled non-alcoholic sherbet of saffron, rosewater and sugar, sometimes with basil seed or sekanjabin vinegar syrup. Yazd's answer to 45C afternoons.

places.name: Bagh-e Dolat Abad teahouse
places.note: Garden teahouse under the tallest windcatcher; sharbat and Persian chai in the shade.

places.name: Silk Road Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Courtyard cafe pouring sharbat and tea all afternoon; popular traveller hangout.

places.name: Amir Chakhmaq Square confectioners
places.note: Sell bottled sharbat syrups and cold glasses to drink on the spot.

landmarks: Historic City of Yazd
A UNESCO-listed labyrinth of sun-baked adobe lanes, windcatchers and covered passageways—one of Earth's oldest continuously inhabited desert cities.
Jameh Mosque of Yazd
Iran's tallest pair of minarets soars above a dazzling blue-tiled portal, crowning this 14th-century Friday mosque of the desert.
Amir Chakhmaq Complex
A three-tiered facade of sunset-lit alcoves overlooking the main square, iconic backdrop for Yazd's dramatic Muharram mourning ceremonies.
Towers of Silence (Dakhmeh)
Twin hilltop towers where Zoroastrians once laid out their dead beneath the sky, hauntingly ringed by desert and abandoned ossuary buildings.
Zoroastrian Fire Temple (Atashkadeh)
Home to a sacred flame said to have burned continuously since 470 AD, the spiritual heart of the world's Zoroastrian community.
Dowlat Abad Garden
A UNESCO Persian garden whose 33-meter badgir—the world's tallest windcatcher—cools a jewel-box pavilion of stained glass and stucco.
Yazd Water Museum
Set in a merchant's mansion, it unravels the ingenious qanat tunnels that carried mountain water beneath the desert for millennia.
Alexander's Prison (Ziaiyeh School)
A 15th-century domed madrasa nicknamed for a legendary dungeon mentioned by Hafez, with a deep well and exhibits in its courtyard.
Fahadan Quarter
Yazd's oldest neighborhood, where rooftop cafés survey a skyline of mud-brick domes, badgirs and the distant snows of Shir Kuh.
Chak Chak (Pir-e Sabz)
Zoroastrianism's holiest mountain shrine drips spring water inside a cliff-clinging grotto, a spectacular pilgrimage drive through the desert from Yazd.

dom.op: Raja Passenger Trains (Islamic Republic of Iran Railways)

train.note: No international trains. Yazd sits on the main Tehran-Kerman line, which makes it one of the better-connected Iranian cities by rail: overnight trains reach Tehran in about 7 hours and services run to Isfahan, Kerman and Mashhad. The station is a short taxi ride from the old town. Book through a hotel or agent, as Raja's site does not accept foreign cards.

bus.note: No international coaches. Yazd's terminal has VIP coaches to Isfahan (about 4 hours), Shiraz (6), Tehran (8-9) and Kerman (5), run by Seiro Safar and Hamsafar. Buy at the terminal in cash - carry rials, since foreign bank cards do not work anywhere in Iran.

ferry.note: Yazd sits between two deserts on the central plateau with no water at all, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Meybod
half.blurb: Desert town with a restored caravanserai, an ice house, and a pigeon tower built for collecting fertilizer.

half.name: Kharanaq
half.blurb: Abandoned mud-brick village of stacked adobe houses connected by narrow covered alleys.

half.name: Abarkuh
half.blurb: Small town home to one of the world's oldest living trees, a cypress estimated at over 4,000 years old.

full.name: Isfahan
full.blurb: Historic Persian capital centered on the vast Naqsh-e Jahan Square, ringed by tiled mosques and palaces.
